paras: The Montevideo courthouse crowd of November 1903 was a reported mob threat against Joe Scott, a Black prisoner, when he was brought to Montevideo, Minnesota, on November 24, 1903, to answer for an axe attack on Helen Olson at Watson the previous July. Scott pleaded guilty and was sentenced to thirty years, and the sheriff removed him from the town under guard. Whether a mob threatened him is disputed: the St. Paul Globe described a "threatening mob" that followed him to the train, while dispatches from Montevideo reported no disturbance.

In July 1903 Helen Olson was struck with an axe during a robbery of her father's house at Watson, and Scott was captured by armed searchers after being shot in the arm. The Globe wrote that only the vigilance of the sheriff had kept a mob from lynching him at the time of his capture, and he had since been held in the Glencoe jail.

Sheriff Hartley brought Scott from Glencoe to Montevideo on the afternoon of Tuesday, November 24, to answer three indictments for robbery, assault and burglary in the first degree. According to the Minneapolis Journal's Montevideo correspondent, "A large crowd gathered at the station, but there was no demonstration," and Scott was taken directly to the courthouse. After conferring with appointed counsel, Attorney Gjerset, he pleaded guilty to all three, asked for mercy, and received ten years on each, thirty years in all.

The Journal reported that within an hour of arriving Scott was in the county jail "under a heavy guard," where hundreds of people visited him and he told the correspondent he had expected to hang. The Globe's St. Paul account instead said that a mob filled the courthouse and crowded the streets, and that Sheriff Hartley and several deputies, fearing a lynching attempt, took Scott to St. Paul on the first train while a threatening mob followed them to it. Scott himself told the Globe that "when I got sight of the mob" he decided to plead guilty.

Scott was held in the Ramsey County jail in St. Paul on his way to the state prison at Stillwater. There he gave the Globe a confession describing the robbery and the axe blow, insisting the crime was not premeditated. Montevideo dispatches said the sentence met with general approval and that even Olson's relatives were satisfied; no arrests or official action concerning the crowd were reported.

Most white papers treated the case as a court story, under headlines such as "Gets Thirty Years" and "Negro Gets Thirty Years" that identified Scott by race. The Globe's own Montevideo special of November 24 said "There was no disturbance," and that dispatch was reprinted in the Princeton Union and in state-news digests in the Mower County Transcript and Little Falls Herald, which recalled that Scott had been "almost lynched" in the summer. Local notices ran in the Willmar Tribune, Morris Tribune and Milbank Herald-Advance.

The Globe's next-day story, headlined "Convicted Negro Makes Confession," was the only white account to describe a threatening mob, and it framed Scott as relieved to be safe from it. The Minneapolis Journal's editorial page called the sentence "about right" but justice "a little slow," adding that a weekly flogging would make a more adequate penalty, and its news brief called Scott a "Brute."

The St. Paul Appeal, a Black weekly, reported that Scott was moved to St. Paul because there was "still some danger of mob violence" and called his sentence deserved. It also rejected the earlier insinuation of a sexual assault, stating that "There was no attempt to commit rape," and complained that the whole race was made to bear the burden of one criminal's acts.

The two accounts datelined Montevideo, one from the Globe's own correspondent, report a large crowd but no disturbance, while the threatening mob appears only in the Globe's St. Paul story, which drew partly on Scott's own statement, and in the Appeal's mention of danger. The papers also differ on when Scott left Montevideo: the Globe has him leaving on the first train after sentence, while the Journal says he left at noon on November 25 and the Appeal says he was taken to Stillwater on a Sunday.

reader.title: Montevideo courthouse crowd (1903)
bases: The only reported harm is a crowd's threat against a Black prisoner during sentencing and removal, and it is reported by A11 and A16 but contradicted by A8 and A9; no violence occurred.
The Globe's St. Paul story (A11) and the Appeal (A16) report a threatening mob or danger of one, but both Montevideo dispatches (A8, A9) report no disturbance or demonstration.

accounts.gist: Scott was brought at once to St. Paul because there was still some danger of mob violence; no rape had been attempted, despite earlier press insinuation.

framing.detail: Local and state papers ran short court items ('Gets Thirty Years', 'Negro Gets Thirty Years', 'Sentenced to Thirty Years') stressing the speed of justice and community approval.
The St. Paul Globe headlined 'Convicted Negro Makes Confession', printed Scott's statement at length, and described a threatening mob held off by the sheriff's precautions.
A Minneapolis Journal editorial called the sentence 'about right' but justice 'a little slow' and wished the law added a weekly flogging; its news brief called Scott a 'Brute'.
The St. Paul Appeal accepted the sentence as 'deserved' but noted the danger of mob violence, denied the rape insinuation, and protested that the whole race bore the burden of one man's crime.
